turns.content: At a neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine is released by a motor neuron and acts across a synaptic cleft on muscle receptors. Classify this signaling route.

A stimulated T cell releases a growth factor that acts on the same cell and neighboring immune cells. Distinguish the two local signaling modes involved, and explain what evidence would be needed before calling either effect endocrine.
A mammary-gland factor is detected both near its source and in plasma. What observations would distinguish a local paracrine effect from a true endocrine effect at distant tissue?
Circulating thyroid hormone reaches many tissues, yet only some cells change transcription. Explain how receptor expression determines that selectivity.
Turn route, transport distance, producer-responder relation, and receptor availability into a practical classification rule for these signaling modes.
Use that rule to contrast neuromuscular transmission with thyroid-hormone signaling without relying only on the identity of the messenger.
Given only that the T-cell factor acts on its producer and nearby cells, state the most precise classifications supported and the remaining uncertainty.
An investigator calls the mammary factor paracrine even though the claimed response occurs only after bloodstream transport to distant tissue. Evaluate that classification.
Which transport and receptor measurements would resolve whether the mammary factor has a local effect, a systemic effect, or both?
Apply the resulting framework to a pancreatic factor that enters blood and changes gene expression only in receptor-positive liver cells.
